text.p: Argentina's Foreign Minister said in an interview published on Thursday that Spain's arrest warrant for former military ruler Gen. Leopoldo Galtieri was "totally inadmissible" and the "dead are dead."

In an interview with Argentine newspaper Pagina 12 in Paris, Guido Di Tella said "nobody in their right minds" would try to put Galtieri on trial abroad. Spanish High Court Judge Baltazar Garzon, investigating the disappearance of 300 Spaniards in the Argentine military's "Dirty War" in the late 1970s, charged Galtieri with ordering the killings of three of the Spaniards.
"We believe that what Judge Garzon is doing is totally inadmissible, it has no legal base," the minister said. "We will oppose it with our own legal means, it's elementary. What country wouldn't?

"The dead are dead, the horrors surrounding those deaths cannot be compensated," he said. "We find what happened in the last military dictatorship in Argentina horrendous, even the armed forces have said so, but this is a matter for Argentine jurisdiction."

Galtieri, now 70, was president for two years under the brutal 1976-83 military regime that human rights activists say abducted and killed up to 30,000 people. He also ordered the 1982 invasion of the Falklands that led to war with Britain.
But Argentina rules out his extradition on the grounds that he has already been tried for his crimes, convicted, jailed and freed under a general amnesty in 1989.

Garzon ordered Interpol to arrest Galtieri if he leaves Argentina for trial for his alleged role in abducting, torturing and killing Spanish citizen Victor Labrador and his two sons in 1976. Argentine human rights groups such as the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo and Nobel Peace Prize winner Adolfo Perez Esquivel hailed Garzon for helping their "fight against impunity."
Outraged by the amnesty decreed by President Carlos Menem shortly after he came to power, they demand information about the fate of the missing and for the guilty to go back to jail.

But Justice Minister Elias Jassan insisted it was a "closed case," even when urged by French President Jacques Chirac on a recent visit here to let Navy Capt. Alfredo Astiz, "the Blond Angel," be jailed in France for the murder of two French nuns.
